The attacker can eavesdrop on the conversation, maybe even inject their own data into the traffic.

First, I should think about the common methods used in MITM attacks. I know that this often involves some form of network interception. Maybe something like ARP spoofing? Because ARP is used to map IP addresses to MAC addresses. If an attacker can spoof the ARP table, they can redirect traffic between the victim and the target. For example, if the attacker is on the same local network, they can make the victim think that the gateway is the attacker, and vice versa. That way, the attacker can intercept all traffic going to and from the gateway.

Another method could be DNS spoofing. If the attacker can manipulate the DNS records, they can redirect the victim to a malicious site instead of the intended one. So when the user tries to access a website, they're actually being directed to a fake server that the attacker controls. That way, the attacker can intercept the data being sent and received.

Then there's the use of SSL/TLS interception. If the attacker can somehow compromise the SSL certificate, they can act as a man-in-the-middle and decrypt the traffic. But wait, how does that work? Maybe by using a certificate that's trusted by the victim's browser. If the attacker has a certificate that's trusted, they can insert themselves into the communication. But that requires some kind of certificate authority (CA) compromise or maybe using a fake certificate that's installed on the victim's machine.

Another way could be using a rogue access point. If the attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi access point with the same name as a legitimate one, users might connect to it instead of the real one. Once connected, the attacker can intercept all the traffic between the user and the actual network.

Also, maybe using packet sniffing tools. If the attacker can get onto the same network as the victim, they can use tools like Wireshark or tcpdump to capture packets. But that's more of a passive attack. However, if the attacker can actively modify the packets, that's a more active MITM.
